Let $I$ be a nonempty finite totally ordered set, let $d\ge1$, and assign a point $\xi_i\in\mathbb R^d$ to each $i\in I$. A **cluster** is a nonempty subset of $I$. For a cluster $\tau$, write $X_\tau=\{\xi_i:i\in\tau\}$, $\operatorname{diam}(\tau)=\max_{i,j\in\tau}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$, and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)=\min_{i\in\tau,j\in\sigma}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$. These extrema exist because the index sets are finite and nonempty; repeated geometric points are allowed.

A **balanced cluster tree with leaf threshold $b$**, where $1\le b\le |I|$, is the rooted binary tree whose root is $I$, whose children of an internal cluster $\tau$ are its first $\lfloor|\tau|/2\rfloor$ and last $\lceil|\tau|/2\rceil$ indices in the fixed order, and which stops splitting at clusters of size at most $b$. Its two children are disjoint and their union is $\tau$. Row and column index sets may have separate trees and separate point assignments.

Fix an admissibility parameter $\eta>0$. A pair of clusters $(\tau,\sigma)$ is **admissible** when $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)>0$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)\ge\eta\max(\operatorname{diam}(\tau),\operatorname{diam}(\sigma))$. The strict positive-distance condition keeps coincident or intersecting clusters in the near field, including diagonal singleton blocks.

The **block-cluster tree** starts at $(I,J)$. It stops at a pair if that pair is admissible or if both clusters are leaves. Otherwise it splits a nonleaf cluster of larger cardinality; ties are resolved by splitting the row cluster. The children of a split are the corresponding child-cluster pairs. Its terminal pairs are called **block-cluster leaves**. Admissible leaves are **far blocks**; nonadmissible leaves, which have two leaf clusters, are **near blocks**.

derivations.claim: At depth zero the root has size $n=\lceil n/2^0\rceil$. Induction proves the size bound at every depth.
Put $H=\lceil\log_2(n/b)\rceil$. Then $2^H\ge n/b$, so $\lceil n/2^H\rceil\le b$. By step 1.1 every cluster at depth $H$ has size at most $b$ and is a leaf; hence the tree depth is at most $H$.

If a leaf is not the root, its parent has an integer size $m>b$, so the smaller child has size $\lfloor m/2\rfloor\ge\lfloor(b+1)/2\rfloor\ge b/2$. The same lower bound on leaf size holds when the root is a leaf because then there is one leaf and $n\ge b/2$. **Input:** A field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, positive integers $m,n$, a finite factor list $U_s\in\mathbb F^{m\times r_s}$ and $V_s\in\mathbb F^{n\times r_s}$ representing $M=\sum_s U_sV_s^*$, a rank cap $0\le k\le\min(m,n)$, and a Frobenius tolerance $\delta\ge0$. The conjugate transpose $M^*$ and Frobenius norm are those of [[def-finite-tensor-arrays-and-frobenius-inner-product]].

**Procedure:** Concatenate the factors as $U=[U_1\ \cdots\ U_p]$ and $V=[V_1\ \cdots\ V_p]$, so $M=UV^*$. Take compact singular value decompositions $U=Q_UR_U$ and $V=Q_VR_V$, where the columns of $Q_U,Q_V$ are orthonormal and span the respective column spaces. Form the core $C=R_UR_V^*$ and compute an SVD $C=P\Sigma Q^*$. Let its positive singular values be $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_t>0$. Find the smallest $q\in\{0,\ldots,\min(k,t)\}$ for which $e_q:=(\sum_{j>q}s_j^2)^{1/2}\le\delta$. If no such $q$ exists, return **tolerance-not-met**. Otherwise return **success** with factors $\widehat U=Q_UP_{[:,1:q]}\Sigma_q$ and $\widehat V=Q_VQ_{[:,1:q]}$, where $\Sigma_q=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_q)$, and the exact discarded-tail certificate $e_q$; when $q=0$, use empty $m\times0$ and $n\times0$ factors.

$$ \langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{n_d}\overline{A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}B_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}, \qquad \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle_F}. $$
For a matrix, rank means the dimension of its column image and the Frobenius inner product is the same entrywise formula. The adjoint $M^*$ is conjugate transpose (transpose over $\mathbb R$).

For $1\le k\le d$, the mode-$k$ unfolding $A_{(k)}$ has $n_k$ rows and $\prod_{j\ne k}n_j$ columns. Its row index is $i_k$ and its column index is the remaining tuple in increasing mode order, lexicographically ordered. Its entry at that row and column is the corresponding entry of $A$. For $1\le k<d$, the cut-$k$ unfolding $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ has row tuple $(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and column tuple $(i_{k+1},\ldots,i_d)$, each lexicographically ordered. These conventions fix all reshapes used below.

$$ \langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{n_d}\overline{A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}B_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}, \qquad \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle_F}. $$

Its row index is $i_k$ and its column index is the remaining tuple in increasing mode order, lexicographically ordered. Its entry at that row and column is the corresponding entry of $A$. For $1\le k<d$, the cut-$k$ unfolding $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ has row tuple $(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and column tuple $(i_{k+1},\ldots,i_d)$, each lexicographically ordered. Let $I$ be a nonempty finite totally ordered set, let $d\ge1$, and assign a point $\xi_i\in\mathbb R^d$ to each $i\in I$. A **cluster** is a nonempty subset of $I$. For a cluster $\tau$, write $X_\tau=\{\xi_i:i\in\tau\}$, $\operatorname{diam}(\tau)=\max_{i,j\in\tau}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$, and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)=\min_{i\in\tau,j\in\sigma}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$. These extrema exist because the index sets are finite and nonempty; repeated geometric points are allowed.

A **balanced cluster tree with leaf threshold $b$**, where $1\le b\le |I|$, is the rooted binary tree whose root is $I$, whose children of an internal cluster $\tau$ are its first $\lfloor|\tau|/2\rfloor$ and last $\lceil|\tau|/2\rceil$ indices in the fixed order, and which stops splitting at clusters of size at most $b$. Its two children are disjoint and their union is $\tau$. Row and column index sets may have separate trees and separate point assignments.

Fix an admissibility parameter $\eta>0$. A pair of clusters $(\tau,\sigma)$ is **admissible** when $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)>0$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)\ge\eta\max(\operatorname{diam}(\tau),\operatorname{diam}(\sigma))$. The strict positive-distance condition keeps coincident or intersecting clusters in the near field, including diagonal singleton blocks.

The **block-cluster tree** starts at $(I,J)$. It stops at a pair if that pair is admissible or if both clusters are leaves. Otherwise it splits a nonleaf cluster of larger cardinality; ties are resolved by splitting the row cluster. The children of a split are the corresponding child-cluster pairs. Its terminal pairs are called **block-cluster leaves**. Admissible leaves are **far blocks**; nonadmissible leaves, which have two leaf clusters, are **near blocks**.

Let $I$ be a nonempty finite totally ordered set, let $d\ge1$, and assign a point $\xi_i\in\mathbb R^d$ to each $i\in I$. A **cluster** is a nonempty subset of $I$. For a cluster $\tau$, write $X_\tau=\{\xi_i:i\in\tau\}$, $\operatorname{diam}(\tau)=\max_{i,j\in\tau}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$, and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)=\min_{i\in\tau,j\in\sigma}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$. These extrema exist because the index sets are finite and nonempty; repeated geometric points are allowed.

A **balanced cluster tree with leaf threshold $b$**, where $1\le b\le |I|$, is the rooted binary tree whose root is $I$, whose children of an internal cluster $\tau$ are its first $\lfloor|\tau|/2\rfloor$ and last $\lceil|\tau|/2\rceil$ indices in the fixed order, and which stops splitting at clusters of size at most $b$. Its two children are disjoint and their union is $\tau$. Row and column index sets may have separate trees and separate point assignments.

Fix an admissibility parameter $\eta>0$. A pair of clusters $(\tau,\sigma)$ is **admissible** when $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)>0$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)\ge\eta\max(\operatorname{diam}(\tau),\operatorname{diam}(\sigma))$. The strict positive-distance condition keeps coincident or intersecting clusters in the near field, including diagonal singleton blocks.

The **block-cluster tree** starts at $(I,J)$. It stops at a pair if that pair is admissible or if both clusters are leaves. Otherwise it splits a nonleaf cluster of larger cardinality; ties are resolved by splitting the row cluster. The children of a split are the corresponding child-cluster pairs. Its terminal pairs are called **block-cluster leaves**. Admissible leaves are **far blocks**; nonadmissible leaves, which have two leaf clusters, are **near blocks**.
